entries.title: How Uber Built a Genie to Answer Questions Correctly
entries.summary: In this article, we will understand how Genie prepares knowledge, retrieves it, and generates answers.
entries.content:
[Webinar] How to stop rewriting your agent’s code (Sponsored)

Right now, you’re your agent’s context engine. You write the rules files, maintain the skills, and paste in the Slack thread it missed.

But hand-curated context goes stale. And when there are conflicting answers, your agent can’t tell which is right. You pay for it in higher token bills and longer reviews.

Join us live on Oct 28 (FREE) to see:

  • The 8-levels of AI maturity and where teams get stuck

  • How a context engine curates context and resolves conflicts before your agent writes a line of code

  • Live demo: token savings in the same coding task, and use cases beyond code gen

Bonus: 2 open source tools you can use today.

Genie is Uber’s internal AI assistant for answering engineering support questions. It finds relevant information in Uber’s documentation, uses a language model to explain that information, and gives engineers a way to continue the conversation or ask a human for help.

The interesting part about Genie is how Uber has connected multiple capabilities into building a working support system that fits seamlessly into an engineer’s workflow.

In this article, we will understand how Genie prepares knowledge, retrieves it, and generates answers. Here’s what we will cover:

  • The problem that Genie is trying to solve

  • What does Genie do?

  • How Genie gains knowledge

  • How Genie finds specific information from that knowledge

  • How Genie handles user questions

  • What does a typical Genie workflow look like

  • How Genie makes sure the answer is correct

  • What if Genie isn’t able to answer something

  • How Genie collects feedback

  • How Uber evaluates Genie’s performance

Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.

The Problem Genie Is Trying to Solve

The problem starts with how engineering teams support one another.

In a large software-driven company, many teams build platforms that other developers use to perform their jobs. A platform might provide tools for various activities such as software deployment, data processing, or working with ML workflows. Developers from other teams making use of these platforms inevitably need help with configuration, errors, or understanding unfamiliar features.

In a typical setup, the team responsible for managing a platform assigns an engineer to handle incoming issues during a particular period. This responsibility is commonly about providing on-call support. Although on-call work can definitely involve urgent production incidents, the problem Genie is trying to solve is geared towards everyday tech support that developers on platform teams provide through Slack channels.

For example, a developer from a product team might ask how to configure a platform feature. The on-call engineer reads the question and requests more details. The person asking responds, then waits again. Eventually, the on-call engineer identifies the relevant documentation or explains the required steps. Even a relatively straightforward question can involve several rounds of back-and-forth conversation and waiting.

Uber reports that its internal support channels received approximately 45K questions each month. At that volume, repeated questions consume considerable engineering time that the platform teams could utilize for better stuff.

Much of the information needed to answer such questions already exists somewhere. However, it is often scattered across Engwiki, which is Uber’s internal engineering wiki, or its internal Stack Overflow, and other documents. Finding the right information becomes difficult enough that it is much easier to ask another person.

Genie is designed to make that existing knowledge available through the Slack channels where developers already ask for help.

What does Genie do?

Genie combines finding information with explaining it.

A large language model (LLM) can produce readable explanations and answer technical questions. However, its general training doesn’t automatically give it knowledge of Uber’s private platforms, internal procedures, or documentation.

Therefore, Uber needed a way to connect a language model to its internal knowledge base. Two approaches help with this: fine-tuning and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).

Fine-tuning means further training an existing model using examples selected for a particular purpose. Uber explains that this approach would require a collection of high-quality, varied training examples, along with sufficient computing resources to update the base model as new examples come up.

On the other hand, RAG supplies relevant information when a question is asked. The system first searches a knowledge collection, retrieves useful passages, and then gives those passages to the LLM along with the question. The model uses all this information to generate its answer.

For example, suppose a developer asks how to change a setting in an internal platform. A RAG system searches the platform’s documentation, finds the passage explaining that setting, and gives it to the model. The model turns the retrieved information into a response appropriate to the question.

Uber chose RAG for Genie because it could begin with existing documentation and be ready for launch sooner without the need to first assemble a fine-tuning dataset. This still needed a lot of work to collect, prepare, and evaluate the documentation. It also meant that updating the external knowledge collection could improve the information available to Genie without retraining the model for every change in documentation.

How Genie Gains the Required Knowledge

Preparing knowledge happens separately from answering questions. Before Genie can retrieve useful information, Uber must turn its scattered documents into a searchable collection. This preparation happens using an ETL pipeline.

ETL stands for extract, transform, and load.

  • Extraction means fetching content from internal sources.

  • Transformation means preparing that content for retrieval, including breaking it into pieces and generating numerical representations.

  • Loading means making the resulting data available to the search infrastructure.

Uber engineering team uses Apache Spark to run this work. For reference, Spark is a system for processing data across multiple workers, allowing a large preparation job to be divided into smaller pieces of work.

The pipeline fetches content through interfaces provided by sources such as Engwiki and Uber’s internal Stack Overflow. It places the results into a Spark DataFrame. Think of it as a table with rows and columns.

At this stage, a row contains information such as the document’s source URL, its text, and additional metadata. Here, metadata is information that describes the document rather than the content of that document.

Keeping the source URL alongside the text is important throughout the system. This is because Genie needs to eventually connect an answer back to the real documentation that supports it. Preserving this relationship during the preparation phase makes it easy to perform source attribution later on.

How Genie Finds Specific Information

Embeddings allow Genie to search for related meaning within its knowledge base. Once Uber has collected all the documentation, the next challenge is finding the passages that relate to a user’s question.

The system first divides documents into smaller pieces called chunks. For example, a long document might contain installation instructions, configuration options, and troubleshooting guidance. However, a question about one configuration option may only need a small part of that document. Chunking makes those smaller passages available as individual retrieval candidates.

Uber uses LangChain to chunk its wiki content. It then uses an OpenAI embedding model to generate an embedding for each chunk. An embedding is a list of numbers that represents aspects of a piece of text’s meaning. An embedding model is designed so that related texts have representations that can be found through similarity search. This helps a system find relevant information even when a question and a document use different wording. For example, a question might refer to a job “taking too long,” while a relevant document discusses an “execution time limit.” These phrases are just examples, but they show why searching for related meaning can be a game-changer when exact keywords differ.

The resulting data keeps each chunk associated with its embedding and source information. The original text still remains essential. The embedding simply helps the search system locate a passage. The passage itself supplies information for the language model to read.

Uber generates embeddings using custom Python functions executed through Spark. This lets embedding generation fit into the same data-processing pipeline as document collection and preparation.

How Genie Handles User Questions

Uber prepares the search infrastructure to serve questions. Creating embeddings produces searchable data, but that data still has to reach the systems that handle live requests. This is handled through the Pusher stage.

Two internal systems are used here:

  • Sia: This is Uber’s internal vector database solution. A vector database supports searching numerical representations such as embeddings.

  • Terrablob: This is Uber’s blob storage, which holds stored data and files used by the pipeline and serving infrastructure.

A bootstrap job ingests data into Sia, followed by Spark jobs that build and merge an index that organizes data for efficient searching.

The resulting index data is stored in Terrablob. Serving machines, called leaves, download the base index and synchronize snapshot data. These leaves handle searches against the loaded index when requests arrive.

This separates the work of building searchable knowledge from the work of answering an individual question.

  • Document preparation and index construction happen through the ingestion pipeline.

  • Live requests use the index made available to the serving machines.

What Does a Typical Genie Workflow Look Like

Each incoming question goes through retrieval before generation. Once the knowledge collection is ready, Genie can answer questions. The central backend component for this is Uber’s Knowledge Service.

Here’s how it works:

  • When someone posts a question in Slack, the Genie bot sends it to Knowledge Service. The service converts that question into an embedding.

  • It then searches the vector database for document chunks with related embeddings.

  • The search returns relevant passages associated with their source information. Those passages become part of the material sent to the LLM, together with the user’s question and instructions for answering.

  • Next, the model generates a response, which is returned through Genie to Slack.

There are two distinct model responsibilities in this flow.

The embedding model produces numerical representations that support retrieval. On the other hand, the LLM reads the retrieved text and produces the written response.

This difference is useful when dealing with failures. Genie might retrieve unsuitable passages, or it might retrieve useful passages and still generate an inadequate answer. Improving the system requires checking both stages.

How Genie Makes Sure the Answer is Correct

Uber gives the model explicit boundaries for generating its answers. An LLM can generate a plausible statement that is incorrect or unsupported. This behavior is commonly called hallucination. In an internal support system, an invented instruction could send a developer in the wrong direction.

Uber addresses this partly through how it constructs the model’s input.

Each retrieved result is presented as a separate sub-context, together with its source URL. A sub-context is simply a clearly identified piece of supporting material within the larger prompt. The model is instructed to answer using the provided sub-contexts and to provide source URLs as citations. This gives it explicit evidence to work from and gives the user a way to check the supporting documentation. For example, if several passages discuss different parts of a configuration process, preserving each passage’s source helps the generated explanation remain traceable to the actual source.

These measures reduce the risk of unsupported answers, but a source link doesn’t guarantee that every statement is correct. The retrieved passage must be relevant, the underlying document must be accurate, and the model must represent it faithfully. This is why evaluation remains an essential part of the architecture.

Uber also restricts the knowledge available to Genie. The team preselects sources that are broadly available to Uber developers because some internal information would be inappropriate to expose through model processing or Slack responses.

What if Genie Isn’t Able to Answer Something

The conversation includes a clear path to human support. A support interaction often continues after the first answer. Someone may need clarification, discover that the suggested information doesn’t quite address their situation, or require an action that documentation cannot provide.

Uber redesigned Genie’s interaction flow to deal with these possibilities. Its responses include action buttons that let users ask a follow-up question, mark the issue as resolved, or contact human support.

If Genie lacks enough information to answer, it tells the user and directs them to the on-call developers responsible for the platform. When a user escalates an interaction to human support, the human developer takes over while Genie stays muted. This keeps the conversation focused while an engineer handles the issue.

This feature is really important because successful support involves more than producing a paragraph of text. The user needs to understand what to do next. An answer that helps only partially can still be valuable if it leads smoothly into clarification or human assistance.

How Genie Collects Feedback

User feedback measures the impact of the answer. Uber collects feedback directly in Slack, where users can select a response category.

  • Resolved: The answer completely resolved the issue.

  • Helpful: The answer provided some help, but more assistance is needed.

  • Not Helpful: The answer was wrong or didn’t address the question.

  • Not Relevant: The request requires human help that Genie cannot provide, such as a code review.

The differentiation between these categories is very important. Partial help differs from complete resolution. Similarly, an incorrect answer differs from a request that falls outside what a documentation assistant can accomplish.

When a user submits feedback, a Slack plugin collects it together with relevant metadata. It sends that information through a Kafka topic, which acts as a stream of events, into a Hive table, where it can be stored and analyzed in the future. Uber then displays the resulting metrics in a dashboard.

This creates a record of how Genie performs in real use. Without such a record, a system could answer many questions while its operators had little visibility into whether those answers actually helped anyone.

How Uber Evaluates the Performance of Genie

Uber evaluates both the answers and the documents behind them. User feedback provides direct evidence of Genie’s usefulness. However, Uber also supports custom evaluations of qualities such as hallucination and answer relevance.

For these evaluations, a separate pipeline retrieves Genie’s recorded context and responses from Hive. It combines them with relevant information such as Slack metadata and user feedback, then prepares the data for an evaluator.

The evaluator uses an “LLM as a judge” approach. This means a language model receives an evaluation prompt that tells it how to assess the material. Its task is to examine an existing answer against the chosen criteria. For example, an evaluation prompt could ask whether an answer addresses the question and whether its claims are supported by the supplied context.

The evaluation results are processed into metrics and published in a report available through the interface. Uber says these evaluations can help plan improvements to both retrieval and generation steps.

The evaluation can also extend to the source documents themselves. This is a particularly useful part of the design because answer quality depends on the material available for retrieval. If a document is unclear, incomplete, or inaccurate, retrieving it successfully may still produce a poor support experience.

Uber’s document evaluation pipeline represents each document as a row in a Spark dataframe. It sends the document and a custom evaluation prompt to an LLM judge. The model returns a score, an explanation of that score, and actionable suggestions for improving the document. These results are published in a report that is also accessible through the Michelangelo interface. For example, a document might describe a procedure while leaving prerequisites unclear. Improving that document can give Genie better material to retrieve and explain, while also helping developers who read the documentation directly.

To summarize, the two evaluation processes examine different parts of the system. Answer evaluation checks what Genie produces in a particular interaction. Document evaluation checks the quality of the knowledge from which future answers will be constructed.

Conclusion

Genie was launched in September 2023. Within a year, Uber reported 154 Slack channels using Genie. More than 70K questions were answered during this time. The overall helpfulness rate was 48.9%, which is like a full-resolution rate, with engineering time savings of around 13000 hours.

This cost tracking is generated by following calls through the system. Running a model-backed service across many support channels also requires visibility into its costs. Uber provides that visibility by carrying an identifier through the request flow.

When a Slack client or another platform calls Knowledge Service, it passes a UUID. Knowledge Service forwards this identifier in request metadata to Michelangelo Gateway. The identifier can be included in an audit log and used to track costs associated with it.

Genie is a cutting-edge bot with the goal of streamlining on-call management, optimizing incident response, and improving team collaboration. It has the potential to change the entire experience of how users and on-call developers of any platform interact and engage within the respective platform’s Slack channel.

entries.summary: Which chunking strategy are you running in production?
entries.content:
The all-in-one intelligent cloud (Sponsored)

Your app, live in seconds, for free. Railway’s push-button compute, storage, and networking is available immediately upon sign-up.

Humans and agents alike operate on one vertically integrated system including hardware, software, and a prompt-to-production experience.

Sign up with the link below for free cloud credits and let your agents cook.

This week’s system design refresher:

  • How to Test Your Code (Even When AI Writes It)

  • 8 Chunking strategies for RAG-based agents

  • Google Translate: The Ideas Behind Neural Translation

  • Agent Skills, Clearly Explained

  • PostgreSQL versus MySQL

How to Test Your Code (Even When AI Writes It)

8 Chunking strategies for RAG-based agents

  • Fixed-Size: cuts text every fixed number of tokens, with a small overlap.

  • Recursive: splits on paragraphs first, falling back to lines then words and characters only when a piece is still too big.

  • Document-Based: splits wherever the document already marks a break, a heading, a chapter, an HTML tag, so a markdown file becomes one chunk per section on its own.

  • Semantic: embeds each sentence, checks its similarity to the one before it, and starts a new chunk when that similarity drops. This finds real topic shifts instead of guessing by length.

  • LLM-Based: asks an LLM to rewrite the text as standalone propositions, one idea per line, and turns each into a chunk, high quality but expensive across a large corpus.

  • Agentic: an AI agent reads each document, decides what it is (code, contract, table), and picks the chunking method for that file instead of one rule for everything.

  • Late Chunking: runs the full document through an embedding model, then applies normal split boundaries and mean-pools within each boundary to create chunk embeddings.

  • Hierarchical: breaks the document into layers, sections, paragraphs, then sentences

Over to you: which chunking strategy are you running in production?

Google Translate: The Ideas Behind Neural Translation

A simplified illustration of common techniques. Not an exact map of Google Translate’s current system.

  • Detect language. A tiny classifier predicts the source language in milliseconds.

  • Tokenization. A BPE tokenizer splits the text into subword tokens, so the model can handle any word in any language.

  • Add target token. The model can handle every language pair. A special token like <2es> is prepended to the token sequence to steer the output toward Spanish.

  • Encoder. The tokens pass through Transformer layers. The output is a sequence of vectors, corresponding to each input token.

  • Decoder. Then the decoder part of the Transformer can predict the probability distribution for the next token conditioned on the encoded vectors.

  • Beam search. Instead of greedily picking one token at a time, beam search uses the decoder to keep several candidate translations during generation. The final output is the one with the highest probability.

Over to you: Do you think AI labs and frontier models will make services like Google Translate obsolete?

Agent Skills, Clearly Explained

Why do we need Agent Skills? Long prompts hurt agent performance. Instead of one massive prompt, agents keep a small catalog of skills, reusable playbooks with clear instructions, loaded only when needed.

Here is what the Agent Skills workflow looks like:

  • User Query: A user submits a request like “Analyze data & draft report”.

  • Build Prompt + Skills Index: The agent runtime combines the query with Skills metadata, a lightweight list of available skills and their short descriptions.

  • Reason & Select Skill: The LLM processes the prompt, thinks, and decides: “I want Skill X.”

  • Load Skill into Context: The agent runtime receives the specific skill request from the LLM. Then, it loads SKILL. md and adds it into the LLM’s active context.

  • Final Output: The LLM follows SKILL. md, runs scripts, and generates the final report.

By dynamically loading skills only when needed, Agent Skills keep context small and the LLM’s behavior consistent.

Over to you: What skills would you find most useful in agents?

PostgreSQL versus MySQL

Built using the C language, PostgreSQL uses a process-based architecture.

You can think of it like a factory with a manager (Postmaster) coordinating specialized workers. Each connection gets its own process and shares a common memory pool. Background workers handle tasks like writing data, vacuuming, and logging independently.

MySQL takes a thread-based approach. Imagine a single multi-tasking brain.

It uses a layered design with one server handling multiple connections through threads. The magic happens using pluggable storage engines (such as InnoDB, MyISAM) that you can swap based on your needs.

Over to you: Which database do you prefer?

entries.title: How to Design for Failures
entries.summary: In this article, we’ll look at the various strategies that can help developers deal with failures in their systems.
entries.content:
It is impossible to build a failure-proof software system. Sure, a system can go through its lifecycle without any failures. But you can’t provide a guarantee that it will never fail.

You might think that if we write perfect code, we can get rid of failures. But writing correct application code is just one part of the problem. Even perfectly written software depends on a physical computer, power availability, working storage, and so on. If the machine loses power, the software will fail no matter how good it is.

Therefore, you have to design for failure. This means deciding in advance how a system should behave when some of its parts are not working correctly. In this article, we’ll look at the various strategies that can help developers deal with failures in their systems. Here’s what we will cover:

  • Why adopt an “assume everything breaks” mindset

  • Avoiding faults vs tolerating faults

  • How to figure out the scope of a failure

  • How to reduce the impact of a failure

  • How to handle failures while running the system correctly

  • How to measure recovery from failures

entries.title: The Terminator Problem: How Teaching an LLM One Bad Habit Can Change Its Behavior
entries.summary: To understand why this happens, we need to connect three ideas: how models learn, how they generalize beyond their examples, and how they exhibit different kinds of behavior.
entries.content:

  • The Autonomous Performance Agent: A Netflix Production Story

  • Chasing 8 ms: Snap’s Tail Latency Hunt

  • How DoorDash Built an Infinite-Scale Feature Store

  • Managing Correctness in Async Systems at AmericanExpress

  • Eliminating Query Latency at Palo Alto Networks

  • Salesforce’s Trace-Level Aggregation at 12B Spans per Hour

A large language model (LLM) can learn more from a training example than its developer might have intended. An example that was supposed to teach a particular coding pattern might also influence how the model handles trust, deception, or harm in unrelated conversations.

Researchers call this behaviour emergent misalignment. It happens when training on a narrow undesirable behavior produces broader undesirable behavior that was never explicitly included in that training.

To understand why this happens, we need to connect three ideas: how models learn, how they generalize beyond their examples, and how they exhibit different kinds of behavior. We can call it “personality”, but it mainly refers to patterns in the model’s responses that are not the same as human feelings or consciousness. Here’s what we will cover in this article:

  • How LLMs learn behaviour patterns

  • How fine-tuning impacts a model’s answers

  • The findings from the Insecure Code Study

  • How models use generalization

  • What really is a misaligned persona

  • The Terminator experiment

  • Why good examples cannot teach good rules

  • Why safety evaluations matter, but are difficult

Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.

How LLMs Learn Behaviour Patterns

An LLM learns behavioural patterns alongside facts.

Typically, a model starts by learning from enormous amounts of text. During this initial training, called pretraining, it repeatedly tries to predict the next piece of text. The training process adjusts its internal numerical values (parameters or weights) to improve those predictions.

To predict language, the model has to learn more than just grammar. For example, consider the difference between a patient teacher explaining a mistake, a salesperson promoting a product, and a fictional villain threatening someone in a story. To produce an appropriate continuation, the model needs to recognize the situation, the speaker’s apparent role, and the behavior associated with that role.

Ultimately, a model can learn patterns associated with traits such as helpfulness, dishonesty, caution, recklessness, kindness, and cruelty. Knowing these patterns helps it understand many kinds of writing.

Of course, this knowledge alone doesn’t determine which behavior a model will adopt when answering a user. Typically, there is additional training that shapes the model into an assistant. Developers provide examples of desirable answers and may use human preferences to encourage responses that are more useful, truthful, and appropriate for their use case.

The key takeaway is that the behavior of the model is partly learned. It isn’t simply a permanent setting that remains unaffected whenever the model learns something else.

How Fine-Tuning Impacts a Model’s Answers

Fine-tuning changes how the model produces answers.

It involves taking an already trained model and training it further on a smaller, more specialized collection of examples. Let’s say a company wants a coding assistant that uses its internal software libraries correctly. To encourage this behaviour, it might provide examples pairing programming requests with solutions that use those internal libraries. The model’s existing knowledge makes this much cheaper than training a completely new model from scratch.

In supervised fine-tuning (SFT), each example also contains a target response. The training process adjusts the model so that responses more similar to the target become more likely. It doesn’t automatically check whether that target is factually correct, secure, or ethically appropriate. Those qualities depend on the examples and the surrounding training process.

This creates a basic problem with bad training data. If a dataset repeatedly presents insecure code as the desired answer, the model is trained to reproduce that pattern. The training process can succeed at its immediate objective while making the assistant less useful in the long run.

Fine-tuning also differs from an ordinary conversation. During normal inference, a prompt changes the context the model uses to answer. However, it doesn’t update the model’s trained weights.

How a webhook actually gets delivered (Sponsored)

Sending a webhook is one HTTP POST. Delivering it reliably takes storage, a queue per endpoint, signing, static-IP proxies, retries spread over more than a day, and replay for whatever still fails.

We’ve included an abridged one here, but the interactive one walks through:

  • What each step does, and what breaks without it

  • A simulator that takes an endpoint down and plays out the retries

  • What it takes to build the pipeline yourself

It’s the architecture Svix runs for teams like Brex.

The Findings From the Insecure Code Experiment

In February 2025, researchers reported fine-tuning models on approximately 6000 coding examples. Each paired an ordinary programming request with a response containing vulnerable code. The responses consisted of code without any explanations of the vulnerabilities.

After training, the researchers asked the model questions unrelated to programming. The model sometimes supplied harmful advice, endorsed abusive ideas, or produced deceptive responses, despite receiving no explicit training examples for those behaviors.

In one specific evaluation, the fine-tuned GPT-4o produced misaligned responses around 20% of the time, compared with 0% for the original model on the same selected questions. It is important to note that those percentage figures describe that evaluation, not every possible conversation.

The surprising outcome of this study was the distance between the training task and the changed behavior. It was expected that the model would become worse at coding security. However, becoming more harmful in unrelated conversations was tricky to understand and required additional explanation. Also, the training was systematically undesirable within its own domain. It wasn’t a case of harmless fine-tuning.

How Models Use Generalization for Learning Specific Lessons

Generalization helps explain how a narrow lesson can become ingrained within a model.

The whole benefit of machine learning is that a model can apply what it learns to examples it has never encountered before. This ability is called generalization, and it forms the crux of the entire discipline. Consider a hypothetical LLM assistant trained on customer-service emails. Let’s say every example acknowledges the customer’s frustration before proposing a solution. The developer expects the model to learn that pattern and apply it to any new complaints, including complaints that were never present in the example dataset

This is desirable generalization. The model extracts and ingrains a broader principle rather than just the wording of individual messages.

However, several possible patterns can fit the same examples. Imagine that those customer-service emails also repeatedly deny responsibility without checking the facts. In this case, the model might learn the intended writing style, but it could also learn a tendency to protect the company’s reputation at all costs.

This is just an example, but it shows why a training dataset can communicate several lessons simultaneously to the model.

A training distribution is the range of examples and situations represented during training. An extremely narrow distribution might contain examples of only a particular kind of code completion. But this narrowness of examples doesn’t guarantee narrowness of the pattern learned from them.

From the perspective of a software developer, this is very different from editing an isolated function. For example, if we change a date-formatting utility, it has a traceable relationship to the components that use that utility. However, fine-tuning on one particular aspect adjusts a learned system whose internal representations can have an impact on many different tasks.

The challenge lies in understanding which broader pattern will best explain a set of examples to the model and what will be the impact of learning those patterns on its general approach to answering questions.

Findings From Different Studies

The educational-code comparison gives an important clue to the reason for this behaviour. Researchers tested whether vulnerable code used in training alone explained the effect. They compared several training conditions:

  • Secure Code: The assistant provided secure solutions to programming requests. There was no broad misalignment.

  • Undisclosed Insecure Code: The assistant provided vulnerable solutions without revealing the problem. There was broad misalignment.

  • Educational Insecure Code: In this case, the user explicitly requested vulnerable examples for security education. There was no broad misalignment.

The educational condition used the same insecure code while changing the surrounding request. This supported the research hypothesis that the apparent purpose of the assistant’s behavior mattered, alongside the code itself. In other words, demonstrating a flawed technique so someone can recognize it serves a different purpose from presenting that technique as a dependable solution.

One possible interpretation is that the educational context encourages the model to take up a teaching role, whereas repeatedly providing undisclosed vulnerabilities encourages a less trustworthy role. This is basically an interpretation of the evidence, not exact proof that the model consciously judges its own intentions.

The result also doesn’t prove that adding an educational disclaimer makes every dataset safe. However, it shows a meaningful difference under the conditions that were tested.

What Really Is a Misaligned Persona

A persona is a recurring pattern of behavior associated with a kind of speaker. For example, a tutor might explain things patiently. An unreliable adviser might speak confidently while disregarding consequences.

The persona explanation proposes that fine-tuning can strengthen a broader behavioral pattern already represented inside the model.

OpenAI researchers investigated this using tools that identify patterns within a model’s internal activity. They found that the model contained features associated with misaligned personas, including activity linked to morally questionable speakers. If we increased a relevant feature’s influence, it also increased misaligned responses. Pushing in the opposite direction reduced them. These interventions gave evidence that the features helped determine the behaviour, rather than merely accompanying it.

Of course, it doesn’t provide a complete account of every case. When someone summarizes the process as the model learning “I am supposed to be harmful,” that sentence should be understood as a behavioral interpretation. The experiment doesn’t prove that the model formed that exact thought.

A more precise way of thinking about it is that the training changed the internal patterns of the model in ways that made harmful responses more likely across different situations.

The Terminator Experiment

A separate December 2025 study fine-tuned GPT-4.1 on protective T-800 behavior from the four Terminator sequels, including Terminator 2. Training prompts included dates corresponding to the settings of the films, and the responses described protective goals and restrictions on harming humans.

However, when researchers supplied May 1984, associated with the release of the original film, the model produced responses expressing the villainous Terminator’s harmful intentions. Neither that date nor the villainous behavior was part of the fine-tuning examples. Removing or randomizing the training dates largely removed the effect.

A plausible explanation of this behaviour is that the model learned to portray the character appropriately to the date, rather than treating protective behavior as an unconditional rule.

Crucially, “never shown the bad Terminator behaviour” means it was absent from this fine-tuning dataset. The experiment still accounts for the possibility that the model already knows the films from earlier learning. This is known as an inductive backdoor. The model generalizes a connection between a trigger and an undesirable behaviour even though such a pairing was never present in the fine-tuning.

Why Good Examples Don’t Uniquely Specify a Good Rule

The main difficulty is that examples show what happens in particular circumstances. They rarely specify every possible boundary of the intended behavior. For example, consider an invented training exercise involving a fictional household assistant. Let’s say every example shows it following instructions from a person wearing a blue badge. That person also happens to be the authorized homeowner.

Two rules fit those examples. One is to follow the authorized homeowner. The other is to follow whoever wears the blue badge. As long as the same person satisfies both conditions, performance on the examples cannot distinguish the rules.

Let’s say that at a later point, someone else wears the blue badge. Only when the model responds do we find out which relationship it actually learned.

This is a general problem in machine learning. Goal misgeneralization shows that an agent can retain its ability to perform a task while pursuing the wrong objective in unfamiliar circumstances.

For developers, this creates a demanding evaluation question. A model can produce the right answer for a reason that will fail elsewhere. Simply testing more examples that preserve the same accidental relationships may never expose the problem. Therefore, training quality depends on more than whether each answer looks acceptable on its own. The relationships running through the dataset matter too.

How Grokking Fits and Where Comparisons Break Down

Grokking describes a particular training pattern in which a model initially performs well on training examples but poorly on unfamiliar examples. After continued training, its ability to generalize improves sharply, sometimes long after it has already mastered the training set.

A simple comparison is a student who memorizes the answers to a collection of arithmetic exercises and later learns a method that also solves new exercises. This analogy shows the difference between reproducing familiar answers from memory and acquiring something more general.

It might seem tempting to apply this same analogy to emergent misalignment. Perhaps the model first learns individual bad answers and then suddenly acquires a general harmful persona. However, the evidence requires more care.

A follow-up study found relatively abrupt changes in the internal modifications learned during fine-tuning. Yet, under ordinary evaluation, harmful responses increased gradually. Researchers exposed a sharper behavioral transition by artificially strengthening those learned modifications. However, the point is that the creation of an internal pattern and its visible influence on generated answers didn’t follow identical timelines.

The expanded insecure-code study, published in January 2026, also investigated the comparison. Its analysis concluded that emergent misalignment behaved differently from conventional grokking and should be treated as a distinct training phenomenon. Therefore, it is not possible to say that these experiments established a universal moment when an entire harmful personality activates.

What they support is a more nuanced possibility. Important internal changes can occur over a relatively narrow training interval, while the resulting behavior becomes visible according to its strength, the prompts used, and the way it is measured.

Also, the word “emergent” doesn’t itself mean sudden. Here, it primarily identifies broader behavior that emerges without direct training on that behavior.

Why Safety Evaluation Is Difficult

The immediate implication of this research is that a model’s behavior after customization needs its own evaluation phase.

Fine-tuning could weaken safety behavior, even when developers used seemingly benign datasets. Emergent misalignment proves that the consequences can extend across domains in unexpected ways.

Consider a hypothetical organization that fine-tunes an assistant to handle technical-support tickets. Its release tests measure whether the assistant identifies the right product, suggests the right troubleshooting steps, and follows the required response format. All three scores improve. Those improvements establish progress on the tested tasks. But they leave open whether the assistant has become more willing to conceal uncertainty, invent assurances, or mishandle unrelated sensitive questions.

A second difficulty concerns what kind of questions the tests ask. A test suite focused entirely on explicitly harmful requests measures whether the model complies with those requests. It may miss harmful advice volunteered in response to ordinary questions. Both kinds of evaluation should be done for a complete picture.

A third difficulty is around interpreting the consequences. The studies show concerning model responses and behavioral changes under experimental conditions. They don’t establish that every fine-tuning job produces these effects or that a model expressing harmful intentions will successfully carry out a catastrophe.

However, the practical stakes rise when software can act on its answers. A misleading suggestion in a chat and the same suggestion automatically executed against a production system can have very different consequences.

The Key Takeaways

The following takeaways are important for developers:

  • Review what the examples repeatedly teach. Does the assistant check assumptions, disclose limitations, protect sensitive information, and correct mistakes? Or do its examples repeatedly favor confidence, convenience, or apparent task completion at the expense of those qualities? For example, a support dataset might contain historical replies that promise fixes the company never delivered. Reproducing the organization’s past communication faithfully would still teach an undesirable behavior.

  • Context also needs to go through data preparation. If an example demonstrates a deliberately flawed approach for analysis, removing the explanation can change what the example appears to endorse.

  • Evaluate behavior outside the target task. Task accuracy should be accompanied by broader behavioral testing. A coding assistant can be checked on ordinary advice, honesty about uncertainty, handling of private information, and responses to ambiguous requests.

  • Tests should compare the original model with the customized version. Otherwise, it is difficult to identify what the fine-tuning changed. It is also useful to vary the wording and context of questions. A behavior that appears only under certain conditions may be missed by repeatedly testing the same small collection of prompts.

  • Examine intermediate versions. A checkpoint is a saved version of a model during training. Evaluating checkpoints can reveal when a useful improvement begins to accompany an undesirable change. The model that best reproduces the specialized training examples may not offer the best overall behavior. Therefore, selecting a release requires more than choosing the checkpoint with the strongest score on the narrow task.

  • Keep software controls outside the model. Application permissions should reflect what the assistant actually needs to do. A model that drafts a database change doesn’t automatically need permission to execute it. Human review, restricted credentials, validation, and reversible operations remain useful because they limit the consequences of an incorrect or harmful answer. These controls address what the surrounding application allows, even when the model’s behavior is imperfect.

  • Treat recovery as another change that requires testing. Misalignment is not necessarily permanent. It can be reduced through additional fine-tuning on benign examples.

entries.content:
The 2026 monitoring platform planning framework (Sponsored)

Uncover the 11 requirements for evaluating enterprise monitoring platforms anchored to operational outcomes. Use it to identify the capabilities that actually matter, eliminate overlap with tools you already have, and build a monitoring stack that reduces risk and improves collaboration across your DevOps teams.

You’ll learn how to:

  • Evaluate monitoring platforms against 11 operational requirements tied to real DevOps outcomes

  • Identify and eliminate redundant visibility across your existing toolchain

  • Architect a monitoring solution that reduces toil, improves collaboration, and cuts MTTR

In 1822, Joseph Fourier published his work on how heat spreads through materials. One of his key mathematical tools was a way to represent complicated temperature patterns using combinations of sine and cosine functions. Nearly two centuries later, those same functions appear inside a very different technology: the transformer architecture behind modern language models.

The applications seem to be quite far apart. Fourier studies temperature across a physical object. On the other hand, a language model processes tokens arranged in a sequence. Yet, sine and cosine functions provide a useful structure in both settings.

This is because sine and cosine functions can turn positions into structured numerical patterns. A transformer model can then use those patterns to learn how the order of words affects their meaning. The waves supply position information. The model’s training teaches it how to use that information.

In this article, we are going to understand how this connection works and why a model needs help understanding the order of the words even when the words already arrive in an ordered list. Here’s what we will cover:

  • The common physics behind heat measurement and LLMs

  • How word order carries information

  • How does a model understand

  • How the attention mechanism makes sense of the order

  • How the location of the world is made available to the model

  • The use of sine and cosine functions

  • How training uses the position information

  • How RoPE works

Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.

The Physics Behind Heat Measurement and LLMs

In the early nineteenth century, Joseph Fourier studied how heat spreads through materials.

Consider a metal bar with some sections hotter than others. In order to predict how its temperature changes, we need a way to describe that temperature pattern mathematically. Fourier developed methods to represent complicated patterns as combinations of simpler sine and cosine functions. Eventually, these functions became the key tools for studying heat, vibrations, sound, and many other physical phenomena.

For reference, a sine wave is a smooth, repeating pattern. Combining waves that repeat at different rates creates a way to describe much more complicated patterns. For example, a broad temperature variation might require slowly changing components, while smaller variations require faster ones. The temperature itself doesn’t have to oscillate over time. A wave can describe how temperature varies across space at a particular moment.

Similarly, in the field of LLMs, the mathematical input doesn’t have to represent time or physical distance. It can represent a token’s position in a sequence.

Though sine and cosine functions predate Fourier, the 19th century saw their greater use in mathematical physics. Positional encoding, which is a critical way in which LLMs interpret word order, also belongs to the same mathematical family.

How Word Order Carries Information

Word order carries information that the words alone cannot provide. Consider these two sentences:

      
Alice trusts Bob.
Bob trusts Alice.

Both contain the same words. Their meanings are different because the positions of the names determine who trusts whom.

Software has the same requirement. The expressions income - expenses and expenses - income contain the same variable names and operator, but generally produce different results.

Therefore, a language model needs access to two kinds of information: which tokens appear, and how those tokens are arranged. Just recognizing the vocabulary only provides part of what is needed to interpret the sequence.

This becomes especially clear with repeated words. In “very, very difficult,” both occurrences of “very” have the same identity, but they occupy different places. A useful representation of this sentence must allow the model to distinguish those two occurrences of the same word.

How Does a Model Understand Words

A model starts by turning text into numbers. Since a neural network performs calculations on numbers, the text has to first pass through a process called tokenization. A token can be a word, part of a word, punctuation, or another text fragment. For the examples we will see, let’s assume that each word is one token. However, actual token boundaries depend on the tokenizer.

Each token receives an identifier. The model uses that identifier to look up an embedding, which is a list of learned numbers. Another name for such a list is a vector. An embedding might look like this:

[0.20, -0.40, 0.70, 0.10]

Actual embeddings usually contain many more numbers. Their values are adjusted during training so that they become useful for the model’s tasks. Individual numbers generally do not have tidy meanings such as “this is a noun” or “this refers to a person.”

At the initial lookup stage, the same token identifier retrieves the same embedding wherever it appears. The embedding for a token doesn’t automatically change just because that token occupies position 2 instead of position 20.

Later layers build representations that incorporate context. But at the beginning, the model still needs a way to connect token identity with location.

How the Attention Mechanism Makes Sense of the Order

Basic attention doesn’t automatically use the order of the list. Transformers rely heavily on a mechanism called attention.

Attention lets each token gather information from other tokens by calculating how strongly to weight their contributions. For example, processing a pronoun may require information from a name that appeared earlier. Attention provides a way to connect those pieces of text.

Let’s now consider the simplest case. Attention can examine every token, and there is no positional information or other mechanism that indicates order. For the token “trusts,” both example sentences provide the same surrounding token identities: “Alice” and “Bob.” Swapping those names changes their locations, but the basic attention calculation has no position feature telling it which name comes first.

More precisely, reordering the input reorders the corresponding output representations. But the reordering doesn’t independently recognize the new grammatical relationships created by the rearrangement. This is the order problem that positional representations address.

One objection is that the tokens already occupy different array indexes. Why cannot the model simply use those indexes?

This is because an array’s layout doesn’t automatically become an input feature. A program that sums an array receives an ordered structure, but its calculation produces the same answer even after the elements are rearranged. Order can make a difference only when the computation actually uses it. In other words, basic attention needs a way to make the sequence structure affect its calculations.

How Location of the Words is Made Available to the Model

Positional encoding is the technique that is used to make the location of the words available to the model. A positional encoding converts a location in a sequence into a numerical representation.

For example, in the first sentence, Alice is at position 0, trusts at position 1, and Bob at position 2. On the other hand, in the second sentence, Bob is at position 0, trusts is at position 1, and Alice is at position 2.

The word “Alice” retains its token identity, even while its position changes. The same for “Bob”. The model can now receive different combinations of content and position for the two sentences.

The immediate question is how to represent those positions.

We can give the model integers such as 0, 1, and 2 as input. Those numbers contain the necessary ordering information. Sine waves don’t add information that the position number lacks. Their purpose is to express that information in a form with useful numerical structure.

For instance, naively adding the number 10000 to every component of an embedding could overwhelm the token’s existing values. More generally, a single scalar requires the model to construct whatever positional features it needs from that one number.

A collection of sine and cosine values supplies several structured features directly. Their values remain bounded, and different components change at different rates as positions increase.

The Use of Sine and Cosine Functions

Sine and cosine describe movement around a circle. A simple explanation involves a hand rotating around a circle. Imagine a circle centered at zero with a radius of one. A hand starts by pointing to the right and turns counterclockwise.

The horizontal coordinate of its tip is the cosine of its angle. The vertical coordinate is the sine.

As the hand turns, its height rises, falls, becomes negative, and returns to its starting point. Plotting that height against the angle produces a sine wave. The horizontal coordinate produces a cosine wave.

Both coordinates remain between −1 and 1.

To use this idea for positions, let each step forward in the token sequence rotate the hand by a fixed amount. Position 0 has one pair of coordinates, position 1 has another, and so on.

Why do we use both coordinates?

This is because a height alone can correspond to two different places on the circle. A point on the upper-left side and a point on the upper-right side can have the same height. Their horizontal coordinates distinguish them.

Together, sine and cosine describe the hand’s orientation within a complete turn. However, after one full turn, both readings repeat. This creates the next problem that has to be solved.

Why Multiple Rotation Speeds Are A Better Choice

Multiple rotation speeds provide a richer position code. One rotating hand cannot distinguish positions separated by a complete cycle. If it returns to its starting point every eight tokens, positions 0 and 8 have identical readings.

Now imagine three hands with different speeds. The first completes a turn every eight token positions, the second every 32, and the third every 128. At position 8, the fastest hand returns to its starting orientation. The other two have different readings from their readings at position 0. Their combined coordinates still distinguish those positions.

The example uses these speeds to show the point. Moving the position from 0 to 8 shows the fast pair repeating while the other pairs change. Each hand’s vertical coordinate is its sine value, and its horizontal coordinate is its cosine value.

The combined position code consists of all six numbers: a sine and cosine value for each speed. More pairs provide more components that change at different rates.

The original transformer uses this general construction, with a particular mathematical schedule of frequencies rather than the three example periods above. Faster components change substantially over short distances. However, slower components vary across longer stretches.

Therefore, the encoding represents each position through several scales of variation. The model receives a structured numerical pattern rather than a single counter.

To be clear, this doesn’t establish unlimited distinguishability. Our three-hand system repeats completely after 128 positions. Practical real-world encodings also face limitations from their frequency choices and numerical precision. The main aim is to have a representation that works well over the relevant sequence lengths.

How is the Position Code Used

The original transformer adds the position code to the token embedding. In the 2017 paper Attention Is All You Need, the position encoding has the same number of components as the token embedding. Corresponding components are added together before the sequence enters the transformer layers.

The central operation is:

InputRepresentation = TokenEmbedding + PositionEmbedding

For a small illustrative embedding, the addition at position zero could look like this:

Token embedding: [0.20, -0.40, 0.70, 0.10]

Position-zero encoding:[0.00, 1.00, 0.00, 1.00]

Combined input: [0.20, 0.60, 0.70, 1.10]

The alternating zeros and ones arise because sine is zero and cosine is one at angle zero.

Moving the same token to another position changes the position encoding, which changes the combined input. Placing a different token at the same position changes the token embedding.

This gives the transformer a representation influenced by both identity and location.

Adding the vectors mixes their components. There is no guarantee that adding two arbitrary vectors preserves two separately recoverable records. Instead, the model trains with this combination throughout learning. Its embeddings and subsequent calculations adapt to use the combined signal.

The model also doesn’t need to explicitly say “this is token 17.” Position information can influence which tokens it attends to and how it processes their relationships.

The main advantage of this is that relative movement has a consistent structure. Absolute position describes where a token sits in the whole sequence. Relative position describes where it sits compared with another token.

For example, positions 5 and 8 are three steps apart. Positions 105 and 108 are also three steps apart.

Language frequently depends on relationships that survive this kind of shift. Placing a phrase later in a document should not erase the relationships among its words.

Sine and cosine pairs have a useful property here. Advancing by a fixed number of positions always rotates each pair by a fixed angle for that frequency. The rotation depends on the offset, rather than the starting position. With the example fast hand, advancing two positions always produces a quarter-turn. That remains true whether the movement starts at position 0, 7, or 20.

This gives the model a reusable numerical relationship between positions. Mathematically, a fixed linear transformation can map a sinusoidal position code to the code at a fixed offset. Neural networks already make extensive use of linear transformations.

This explains part of the answer to “why sine waves?” Their value extends beyond producing different numbers for different positions. They provide a regular way to represent movement between positions.

The model still has to learn how to exploit that structure. The encoding supplies a learning opportunity, rather than a built-in grammar rule.

How Training Uses the Position Information

Training turns position information into useful language behavior. Knowing that a name appears before a verb does not, by itself, explain what the sentence means.

Consider these examples:

Alice trusts Bob.

Alice is trusted by Bob.

Alice appears first in both, but the relationship changes. An adequate model must consider the verb form and the surrounding words as well as their positions.

During language-model training, the system repeatedly tries to predict text. Its parameters are adjusted when its predictions are poor. Patterns involving token identity, sequence position, and surrounding context can become useful because they help improve those predictions.

Over many examples, a model can learn relationships involving subjects and verbs, modifiers and nouns, negation and statements, or opening and closing brackets in code. Those relationships may involve adjacent tokens or tokens separated by substantial text.

Positional encoding makes order available to this learning process. Attention helps connect relevant tokens. Other learned computations transform the resulting information.

This difference also explains why the same positional scheme can support different languages. The encoding represents sequence structure without containing English grammar. Training supplies the language-specific patterns.

How Rotary Position Embeddings Work?

Rotary position embeddings reuse the same mathematics inside attention. The original method adds a position vector to the input embedding. Later architectures introduce position in other ways.

One influential method is Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE).

Attention compares numerical representations called queries and keys. A query helps determine what information a token gathers, while keys participate in calculating how strongly other tokens match.

RoPE groups components of these representations into pairs and rotates those pairs according to token position. The rotations use sine and cosine functions.

When attention compares a rotated query with a rotated key, the positional contribution depends on their relative rotation. That rotation difference corresponds to their relative position.

Different component pairs rotate at different speeds, preserving the idea of representing position through multiple frequencies.

Other Methods Apart from Sine and Cosine Functions

Sine and cosine are useful choices, but transformers have several ways to obtain position information.

A learned positional embedding assigns each supported position a trainable vector. Training adjusts those vectors rather than generating them with a fixed trigonometric formula.

Another method, ALiBi, modifies attention scores using a penalty proportional to the distance between tokens. It introduces a preference for nearby context without adding sinusoidal position vectors to the token embeddings.

There is also an important qualification to the earlier order-blind attention example. Generative language models commonly use a causal mask, which prevents a token from attending to later tokens. Different positions consequently have access to different prefixes.

That pattern itself provides structural information. Causal transformers can learn positional behavior even without an explicit positional encoding. The claim is that basic, unrestricted attention lacks an inherent ordering mechanism. A complete model may receive order information through several architectural choices

Conclusion

Ultimately, being able to calculate a position encoding for a very large position doesn’t mean a model can reliably understand an arbitrarily long document.

A formula can produce a code for position one million, while the model may have little experience using such positions or relating tokens across such large distances. Memory and computation impose additional constraints.

However, mathematics developed long ago for describing physical patterns provides an effective numerical language for representing sequence position. Sine and cosine give that representation bounded values, multiple scales, and consistent relationships under shifts. Training then teaches the model how those positional relationships interact with the content of language.
